content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces an open-set approach to contrastive affinity learning using auxiliary prompts for GCD.  This work introduces a two step contrastive affinity learning framework.  The two objectives are multi-prompt clustering and contrastive affinity learning.  Using a semi-supervised affinity propagation approach, the system chooses reliable pseudo-positive pairs.  Their approach shows some improvement on six generalized GCD benchmarks over baselines including GCD and ORCA variants.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The figures help with some intuition of the differences between various variants.

The performance gains are decent, but not overwhelming.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of generalized category discovery (GCD) by learning visual prompts on top of the pretrained ViT backbone. The proposed method is called PromptCAL, which is a two-stage method. In the first stage, the model is jointly trained with self-supervised and contrastive losses; in the second stage, a KNN-based affinity graph is built to generate pseudo labels for contrastive learning, which is expected to learn better visual prompts. PromptCAL achieves significantly better performance than the compared methods on public datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The proposed method, especially the prompt learning on ViT, seems to be new for the GCD problem.
- Strong performance is obtained on public datasets. 

Weaknesses
- The paper assumes the number of new classes to be known, which is not a realistic assumption in the real world. Vaze et al 2022 provide a method for new class estimation. Will the proposed method be able to handle the case without knowing the class number?
- What is the difference between MPC and VPT? It seems MPC is simply adopting VPT with contrastive learning. If so, why a new name MPC is needed? 
- How the [CLS] and [CLU] tokens are used at inference time, for the unlabelled instances from unknown classes?
- In the method of Vaze et al 2022, the imbalanced Herbarian dataset is also evaluated. How will the proposed method work on this more challenging dataset?
- Minor: the related work is put into Appendix, which seems not very proper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The overall writing is easy to follow though some parts are not clear as mentioned above.
- The idea appears to be interesting and relatively novel in the context of GCD.
- Main implementation details seem included and the code is promised to be released in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the paper introduces an interesting and effective method for GCD. Due to the concerns above on unknown class numbers, missed details, missed datasets, etc, I would not recommend acceptance based on its current shape.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of generalized category discovery (GCD). To solve this problem, the authors propose a two-stage contrastive affinity learning method with auxiliary visual prompts, which can effectively find reliable positive pairs for representation learning. Experiments on several datasets show the benefit of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

+ This paper is well-written and easy to follow. The motivation is clear and the proposed method is reasonable. An interesting problem is studied in this paper.

+ An effective approach is proposed for GCD, which achieves new sota performance on GCD settings.

+ Extensive experiments are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.


Weaknesses

- Despite the high performance, the pseudo-labeling framework is not novel in the community. Also, the affinity propagation is well studied in the community for semi-supervised learning. Recall that, the GCD is also a semi-supervised learning problem.

- The framework (Fig.2) is messy, which leads the readers hard to understand the proposed method.

- Since this paper uses a teacher-student structure, the computation cost is largely higher than the other methods. This leads to unfair comparison. In addition, the computation costs (training time, memory cost, #params) of different method should be reported.

- The improvement is mainly contributed by the pseudo-labeling framework instead of injecting the prompt module. While if we remove the prompt module, the overall novelty of the proposed method is limited.

- Why not use RS, RS+ and NCL to perform positive mining and then train the networks with contrastive learning as this paper? This comparison is missed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality: The overall paper is well-written, except the Fig.2 which is hard to understand.

Novelty: Injecting the prompt module for GCD is novel but it is improvement is limited. On the other hand, although the pseudo labeling strategy achieves large improvement, it is novelty is limited.

Reproducibility: Algorithm or source code is not provided. Since the proposed method is complex, it is hard to reproduce it without source code.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper considers a new, interesting, practical task. The proposed method is effective which leads to new SOTA performance. However, the novelty of the main part of the proposed is somewhat limited. In addition, this paper may lead to unfair comparison to other methods due to using two networks.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
- This paper proposes a new representation learning method for the problem of generalized category discovery. 
- The proposed method, called PromptCAL, consists of two stages of training, namely 1) the multi-prompt clustering (MPC) and 2) Contrastive affinity learning (CAL). 
- Unlike previous works that fine-tune the last block of a pre-trained ViT to transfer to new data, authors propose to use Visual Prompt tuning to adapt the pre-trained (and frozen) network to new data. The prompts are supervised with contrastive losses for better semantic discriminability. 
- Next, a semi-supervised Affinity graph is constructed, followed by affinity propagation to obtain robust pseudo labels for the unlabeled examples. 
- The models are then updated using a contrastive affinity loss that utilizes the pseudo labels to improve the representation capabilities of the network. 
- Authors evaluate their method on standard benchmarks on generalized category discovery and show improvements in most cases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Authors observation that naive fine-tuning of visual prompts often overfits the data, but supervising them improves the semantic discriminative abilities, i.e. MPC, is novel and useful to the community.
- The CAL combines affinity propagation (traditional semi-supervised learning) and teacher-student architectures (popular in semi-supervised learning of deep learning era) and shows that each of these methods can be employed in a synergistic fashion.
- The experiments section is mostly exhaustive and authors support all their claims.

Weaknesses:

Paper Writing: The main weakness according to me for this work is the way it is conveyed. The method section is very hard to follow and requires constant switching between sections to understand what is exactly happening.
- To be more specific, the sequence of stages has been briefly described in the beginning of Sec. 2 but in my opinion, the paper needs a system diagram to clearly show the flow of events. 
- It is not clear what the input and output of each of the stages (MPC and CAL) and the supervisory signals are. For affinity propagation, is it run once for every unlabeled sample in the batch? What is the proportion of unlabeled samples in each batch?  It would make the paper reading experience better if authors can mention upfront what data each stage consumes and what labels it uses.
- My suggestion to the authors would be to 1) Add a system figure that visually describes the flow of events and 2) What are the input/output of each stage (For eg. MPC stage operates on both labeled and unlabeled data. In each batch x% come from labeled data and remaining from unlabeled data etc.).

Notation: I believe that given the density of the work, notation should be given special focus and the paper lacks in that aspect.
- In the section Notation (Sec 2.1), mini batch B contains x, which is referred to as a sample vector. Isn't that supposed to be an image?
- In Eq. 1, it is called an extended contrastive loss but I'm not sure where the key vectors T_k are used in the formula. In the accompanying text it is said P(t_q) and N(t_q) are positives and negative sets, are they derived from T_k?. Why are T_k normalized when they aren't being used anywhere. I'm clearly missing something.
- It is not clear why the MPC stage is called clustering? Since clustering already is a field in itself, calling this stage clustering didn't make sense to me? From what I understand, MPC selects a subset of the prompts, averages them and applies a contrastive loss to improve their discriminability, how is this related to clustering? 
- In affinity propagation section, G_d^{0} = G, but G has not been introduced anywhere. Is it G_c?
- With matrices and vectors T is generally used for transpose, but in Eq. 5 it is the power of the matrix. Researchers who are aware of the field can tell the difference but for first time readers, it is not clear if its transpose or power. 
- It is not clear what the queries for affinity propagation are for graph sampling. Is the affinity propagation step run once for every unlabeled sample in the batch? Again, i
- The CAL stage uses the pseudo labels and also operates on labeled and unlabeled data. It is not clear why the MPC stage has "semi-supervised loss" L_{semi}^{[cls]} but CAL stage is called L_CAL^{[CLS]). MPC just has a self-supervised loss on the unlabeled data while CAL uses pseudo labels obtained on the unlabeled samples to supervise them. In a way this is semi-supervised learning too. I think the nomenclature of losses and section needs special attention.

Experiments: The experiment section is very exhaustive when comparing to the SOTA but the ablation experiments need some more work.
- In Table 3, What happens if naive KNN is used instead of cKNN but with affinity propagation, SemiPriori and SemiCL switched on? Right now its not clear how important cKNN is from the table?
- In row 5 of Table 4, the prompts are not present but SemiCL (CLU) is present? How can you put a SemiCL loss on CLU tokens without prompts? This row has the second best number in the table and it is not clear how can this be performed?
- How much is CAL stage alone contributing to the performance of the method? What happens if one does not do MPC, performs SemiAG and CAL? How much would one lose in the final performance?
- How are the number of prompts decided to be 5? What happens if one uses more (for maybe fine-grained datasets) or less? Do the prompts have anything to do with the number of unknown/novel classes in the unlabeled dataset? Also Table 12 (Appendix D) shows something about using different prompts but it is not clear without text. Why were only 2 prompts used for CLU? What happens if all 5 were used or only if 1 was used?

Minor concerns and questions which are not considered to make the decision:
- Why is CAL loss applied on feature space and SemiCL (from MPC) on embedding space? What happened if all the losses are applied on only feature or only embedding space?
- In problem defintion (Sec 2.1) It is mentioned that in the validation set only samples from Y_l are labeled. How are the novel classes evaluated if only labels from Y_l are available?
- In the Visual Prompt Tuning, is it a deep prompt or a shallow prompt. It sounds like a deep prompt but having that information in the paper helps.
- In Eq 3, the first term is the self supervised component and the second term is the supervised component, but in the paragraph below it, it is written in the reverse order. 
- The prompts are supervised with SemiCL loss in MPC and CAL loss in the CAL stage, but finally for clustering only the CLS token features are used. Why can't the CLS and CLU tokens averaged or concatenated and be used together. The information from CLU tokens is passed on to CLS token via self-attention but what is the reason behind this decision?
- What is \beta? It does not occur in any equation but it is referred to in the implementation details and experiments performed in Table 10 (Appendix).
- In D2, Table corresponding to CIFAR-100 is Table 11 and not Table 12.
- How is the number of diffusion steps (T) decided to be 1? What happens if it is performed for higher orders? Wouldn't the label quality improve? Does T have anything to do with the neighborhood parameter K?
- In the TPG diffusion, the maximum row sum should be strictly less than 1, but G_c is normalized, its row sum would be exactly 1? How do you tackle that?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The proposed work is novel with some interesting insights into the working of visual prompt tuning for object discovery.
- The quality of the work and the experiments is high but the writing quality needs significant improvement.
- The paper is not clear in a few sections related to method and in its current form would be hard to reproduce as it misses a few important details.
content.summary_of_the_review: - Overall the paper proposes a nice method for generalized object discovery with some interesting insights into prompt tuning and combining affinity propagation with knowledge distillation for semi-supervised learning. My weaknesses have 3 main components 1) paper writing 2) notations and 3) experiments. Addressing these limitations is important to reach a broader audience and get attention for the work. I expect the authors to pay equal attention to each one of the subsections to improve my rating of the paper.

content.title: PromptCAL: Contrastive Affinity Learning via Auxiliary Prompts for Generalized Category Discovery
content.TL;DR: Our approach seeks to discover known and unknown classes in the unlabelled datasets using affinity relationships between samples via auxiliary prompts.
content.abstract: Recent advances in semi-supervised learning (SSL) have achieved remarkable success in learning with partially labeled in-distribution data. However, many existing SSL models fail to learn on unlabeled data sampled from novel semantic classes and thus rely on the closed-set assumption. In this work, we adopt the open-set SSL setting and target a pragmatic but under-explored generalized category discovery (GCD) setting. The GCD setting aims to categorize unlabeled training data coming from known or unknown novel classes by leveraging the information in the labeled data. We propose a two-stage contrastive affinity learning method with auxiliary visual prompts, dubbed PromptCAL, to address this challenging problem, which can discover reliable affinities between labeled and unlabelled samples to further learn better clusters for both known and novel classes. Specifically, we first embed learnable visual prompts into a pre-trained visual transformer (ViT) backbone and supervise these prompts with an auxiliary loss to reinforce semantic discriminativeness and learn generalizable affinity relationships. Secondly, we propose an affinity-based contrastive loss based on an iterative semi-supervised affinity propagation process which can further enhance the benefits of prompt supervision. Extensive experimental evaluation on six benchmarks demonstrates that our method is effective in discovering novel classes even with limited annotations and surpasses the current state-of-the-art on six benchmark dataset (with more than 10% on CUB and StanfordCars, and significant margin on ImageNet-100). Our code and models will be publicly released.
